recipe.label: Risograph

traits.medium: three-color risograph-looking architectural illustration with spot-color-like layers
traits.texture: dry grain, translucent overprint-looking overlaps and a subtle consistent edge offset
traits.composition: retain the diagonal roofline, railing and window rhythm; leave broad paper sky
traits.lighting: flat graphic contrast with three restrained colored layers on cream

limitations: No actual spot-color separations, calibrated inks or press-ready print files are generated.
Palette and fine geometry are prompt guidance and require visual review across a series.

assets.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept
Asset type: README style reference; intended use: One reviewed Risograph example for the Art Skill style catalog
Primary request: An upward view of a warm beige building with a diagonal roofline, a slim roof railing and red-trimmed windows in the lower part of the frame, beneath a vast blue sky, a small soft white cloud and a faint rainbow patch. Small foliage sits along the lower edge.
Style/medium: three-color risograph-looking architectural illustration with spot-color-like layers
Color palette: #F3EBD6, #254D78, #CE6354, #C6A047
Materials/textures: dry grain, translucent overprint-looking overlaps and a subtle consistent edge offset
Composition/framing: retain the diagonal roofline, railing and window rhythm; leave broad paper sky; Keep portrait orientation and the original broad framing; one image, no frame or panels
Lighting/mood: flat graphic contrast with three restrained colored layers on cream
Requested output target: 1024x1536, opaque background, png; use only supported tool controls
Avoid: real people; copyrighted characters; logos and brand marks; copied artworks; unrequested lettering
Constraints: Keep the original upward viewpoint, diagonal building line, window rhythm, broad empty sky, small cloud placement and faint rainbow motif. Do not add a sea, mountains, a garden terrace or a sunset.; No added people, brands, characters, captions or signatures; Use only this source photograph as the composition reference; never mix motifs from the other photos
